out.rationale: The authors position their game relative to Irving et al.'s debate game and state what they change (one prover instead of two debaters, and a focus on discovering proof protocols rather than on adversarial debaters lending robustness). Irving et al. define the simplest debate game, in which two agents state answers to a question, take turns making statements, and a judge decides which agent wins. Both records concern game-theoretic set-ups in which agents make statements to convince a judge, but neither bears on the other's claim: the passage only contrasts the two designs and does not say the prover-verifier game is built on debate, and the target is a definition that states no question or result for the source to answer, test, support or challenge, so the link is navigation only. The passage does not claim agreement or conflict with debate results.

text: The authors describe Irving et al.'s debate as a two-player game in which agents exchange statements to convince a judge. They say their prover-verifier game differs by using a single debater (the prover) and by aiming to discover proof protocols, rather than relying on adversarial debaters to lend robustness as Irving et al. expected.
title: Anil et al. recast Irving et al.'s two-debater game as a one-prover game aimed at learning proof protocols
